title: Honest citizenship
hook: Sikhs take part honestly in the life of their countries

segments.voice: Yesterday, hospitality to guests: saanjhivaal, all are sharers. Your line was the door stays open. Who did you treat as a guest when they interrupted you? Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

A jury summons arrives in a plain envelope, and the first thought is how to get out of it. A form asks you to report every bit of income, and there's a small line you could leave blank. A ballot sits on the counter for a week. None of this is dramatic. Nobody will make a film about filling in a form truthfully. But this is where a lot of public life actually happens: in small, boring moments where honesty costs a little and nobody's watching. Sikh teaching has something to say about those moments, and it starts with a line that ranks something above truth itself.
screen: `A JURY SUMMONS, A FORM, A BALLOT.` → `SMALL, BORING, UNWATCHED.` → `ONE STEP FURTHER.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living. Not just believing what's true. Living it, in the dull places. A truthful life includes the tax form. Second, kirat. Sikh teaching asks for an honest living, kirat karni. In a hymn in Raag Sarang, Guru Nanak says the one who eats what they've earned by their own effort, and gives some of it away with their own hand, knows the way. Earn honestly, share freely. That's a description of a good neighbor and a good citizen in one sentence. Third, wherever they live. Sikhs live in many places and take part in public life in many ways: as soldiers and nurses, teachers and drivers, voters and volunteers. You may have seen Sikh volunteers cooking for strangers after a storm or a flood. That's langar leaving the gurdwara and walking into the street. Faith here isn't kept apart from the town; it's how you show up in it. Fourth, the small duties. Honest citizenship is mostly unglamorous. Answering the summons. Filling the form truthfully. Paying the fine you actually owe. Voting, or helping someone get to the polls. Picking up the litter outside your own door. None of these is a sermon. Each one is truthful living, the thing Guru Nanak placed higher still. The line gets tested at the kitchen counter, not the podium.
screen: `TRUTHFUL LIVING IS HIGHER STILL.` · `KIRAT: EARN HONESTLY, SHARE FREELY.` · `LANGAR WALKS INTO THE STREET.` · `THE FORM, THE SUMMONS, THE BALLOT.` · then, large: `HONEST CITIZENS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one civic duty. Settle, and breathe. Run through the small public things you've been putting off: a form, a bill, a registration, a neighbor's request, a meeting you could attend, a report you could make about a broken streetlight. Let one rise to the top. Breathe in, and admit honestly why you've been avoiding it. Breathe out, and decide on the first small step and when you'll take it, today if you can. The bell holds the time.
Honest citizenship. Truthful living, which Guru Nanak placed higher than truth alone, carried into the form, the summons and the street. Today's word.
Your line: honest citizens. Today, do the one civic duty you chose, and do it fully, even the part nobody would check. Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, earning an honest living, and of seva beyond the gurdwara, which can mean volunteering, serving food in times of need, and taking part in the life of their towns and countries.
